title: Special three-arrow hammocks compute hammock mapping spaces
statement:
A model category means a complete and cocomplete category $\mathcal M$ with classes $C,F,W$ of cofibrations, fibrations and weak equivalences. The class $W$ is retract closed and satisfies two-out-of-three, and $(C,F\cap W)$ and $(C\cap W,F)$ are weak factorization systems with functorial factorizations. A weak factorization system consists of factorizations of every map into its two classes, each class being exactly the maps with the diagonal-lifting property against the other. Trivial means also in $W$; an object is cofibrant if its initial map is in $C$, and fibrant if its terminal map is in $F$. Universes may be enlarged. Use the hammock construction $L^H(\mathcal M,W)$ of [lem-coef-hammock-infinity-localization]. For $x,y\in\mathcal M$ define an ordinary category $\mathcal T(x,y)$. An object is a zigzag $x\xleftarrow{p}u\xrightarrow{f}v\xleftarrow{i}y$ with $p$ a trivial fibration and $i$ a trivial cofibration. A morphism from $(u,v,p,f,i)$ to $(u',v',p',f',i')$ is a pair $a:u\to u'$, $b:v\to v'$ satisfying $p'a=p$, $bi=i'$ and $bf=f'a$. Such $a,b$ are weak equivalences by two-out-of-three. Composition is componentwise composition. Reduction of strings of these commutative diagrams gives a simplicial map
$$N\mathcal T(x,y)\longrightarrow L^H(\mathcal M,W)(x,y).$$
This map is a weak homotopy equivalence. Pullback of $p$ along a map $x'\to x$ and pushout of $i$ along a map $y\to y'$ give the endpoint actions on $\mathcal T$; their comparisons with precomposition and postcomposition in $L^H$ commute up to the homotopies represented by the corresponding hammocks. An object with $p=i=1$ is sent to the length-one hammock of $f$. No cofibrancy, fibrancy, enrichment, properness or combinatoriality hypothesis is imposed on $x,y$ or $\mathcal M$.

proof.text: Form $\mathcal T(x,y)$ as stated. If $(a,b)$ is a morphism, $p'a=p$ and $bi=i'$ imply $a,b\in W$ by two-out-of-three. Componentwise composition preserves the three equations. Thus a chain of $k$ morphisms is a width-$k$ hammock with three columns before reduction. By the face, degeneracy and reduction rules of [lem-coef-hammock-infinity-localization], taking its reduction gives a simplicial map $\rho:N\mathcal T(x,y)\to L^H(\mathcal M,W)(x,y)$.

source.place: Definitions 3.1-3.2; verification of the displayed comparison

proof.text: We will use only the following closure properties, all consequences of lifting. Trivial cofibrations are ${}^{\square}F$, so [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure] gives identities, composition and pushout stability. Trivial fibrations are $C^{\square}$. To lift a cofibration against a pullback of such a map, project the lifting square to the original map, take its lift, then pair that lift with the given map to the pullback base; the pullback equation holds because the original lift lies over that base map. For a composite of two right-lifting maps first lift against the second factor using the first factor on the top arrow, then lift against the first factor using that first lift on the bottom arrow. The resulting diagonal solves the original square. Identities lift by the prescribed bottom map. Hence trivial fibrations contain identities and are closed under composition and pullback. These arguments require no properness assumption.

source.place: Remark 3.3; elementary lifting arguments, expanding the closure facts used in Proposition 3.5

proof.text: Use [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus] to form $\mathcal Z=Z_{-+-}(x,y)$ with unrestricted outer weak equivalences. Its full subcategory with left arrow a trivial fibration and right arrow a trivial cofibration is exactly $\mathcal T$; write $J:\mathcal T\hookrightarrow\mathcal Z$. We give a homotopy inverse for $NJ$ rather than assuming a calculus for special zigzags.

source.place: Proposition 3.5, first sentence: comparison with unrestricted three-arrow zigzags

proof.text: For $z=(x\xleftarrow{w}u\xrightarrow{f}v\xleftarrow{t}y)$ in $\mathcal Z$, factor $t$ functorially as $y\xrightarrow{i}v_1\xrightarrow{q}v$ with $i$ a trivial cofibration and $q$ a fibration. Since $t,i\in W$, $q$ is a trivial fibration. Put $u_1=u\times_v v_1$, let $a:u_1\to u$ and $f_1:u_1\to v_1$ be the projections, and set $w_1=wa$. By step 2, $a$ is a trivial fibration; hence $w_1\in W$. The new zigzag $Rz=(w_1,f_1,i)$ lies in $\mathcal Z$. The pair $(a,q)$ defines a morphism $Rz\to z$. Functorial factorization and the maps determined by the pullback projections give a functor $R:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z$ and a natural transformation $R\Rightarrow\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal Z}$. The induced vertical maps lie in $W$ by the two augmentation equations and two-out-of-three. If $z\in\mathcal T$, $w_1$ is a composite of trivial fibrations, so $Rz\in\mathcal T$ too.

source.place: Proposition 3.5, first sentence; explicit right-end normalization

proof.text: Factor $w_1$ functorially as $u_1\xrightarrow{j}u_2\xrightarrow{p}x$ with $j$ a cofibration and $p$ a trivial fibration. Since $w_1,p\in W$, $j$ is a trivial cofibration. Put $v_2=v_1\amalg_{u_1}u_2$, with maps $b:v_1\to v_2$ and $f_2:u_2\to v_2$. Step 2 makes $b$ a trivial cofibration, and then $i_2=bi$ is a trivial cofibration. Set $Sz=(x\xleftarrow{p}u_2\xrightarrow{f_2}v_2\xleftarrow{i_2}y)$ in $\mathcal T$. The pair $(j,b)$ defines $Rz\to JSz$. Functoriality of factorization and the pushout gives $S:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal T$ and $R\Rightarrow JS$. Its vertical maps on morphisms are in $W$ by their outer-arrow equations. Both transformations restrict to $RJ\Rightarrow\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal T}$ and $RJ\Rightarrow SJ$, since step 4 showed that $R$ restricts to $\mathcal T$.

source.place: Proposition 3.5, first sentence; explicit left-end normalization

proof.text: For a natural transformation $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$, a chain $c_0\to\cdots\to c_n$ gives, for every $0\leq k\leq n$, the chain $Fc_0\to\cdots\to Fc_k\xrightarrow{\eta_{c_k}}Gc_k\to\cdots\to Gc_n$. Naturality identifies the common faces of these $n+1$ simplices; identities identify their degeneracies. They triangulate a prism and give a homotopy between the realized nerve maps. Apply this explicit construction to the two transformations in steps 4-5 and their restrictions: $N(JS)$ is homotopic to the identity on $N\mathcal Z$ and $N(SJ)$ to the identity on $N\mathcal T$. Thus $NJ$ is a homotopy equivalence on realization, so induces the required bijections on components and isomorphisms on homotopy groups.

source.place: Proposition 3.5, first sentence; explicit nerve prism argument

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-homotopy-fractions-square-criterion] with $U=C\cap W$ and $V=F\cap W$. These are wide subcategories by step 2. Complete a span whose left leg is in $U$ by its pushout; its new leg is in $U$. If the other input leg is in $W$, the remaining new leg is in $W$ by the equation of the square and two-out-of-three. Dually complete a cospan whose right leg is in $V$ by a pullback; its other projection is in $V$, and the extra weak-equivalence condition again follows from the square and two-out-of-three. Limits and colimits can be chosen functorially by their universal properties. Factor each weak equivalence by the model factorization $C$ followed by $F\cap W$; the first factor also lies in $W$ by two-out-of-three. All three choices have exactly the functoriality and the two extra conditions required by the cited statement. Thus $(\mathcal M,W)$ has the homotopy calculus of [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus].

By [lem-coef-homotopy-fractions-hammock-comparison], the reduction $r:N\mathcal Z\to L^H(\mathcal M,W)(x,y)$ is a weak homotopy equivalence. Step 7 checks its precise homotopy-calculus hypothesis. On every chain in $\mathcal T$, the composite $r\circ NJ$ reduces the same three-column diagram as $\rho$ in step 1, so they are equal as simplicial maps. Step 6 and composition of the induced isomorphisms on homotopy groups now show that $\rho$ is a weak homotopy equivalence.

source.place: Proposition 3.5, second sentence, using Dwyer-Kan Proposition 6.2(i)

proof.text:
For $a:x'\to x$, pull back $p:u\to x$ to $p':u'=x'\times_xu\to x'$; its projection $u'\to u$ is denoted $c$. Step 2 keeps the result in $\mathcal T(x',y)$. Compare the following rows of length five:
$$x'\xleftarrow{p'}u'\xrightarrow{c}u\xleftarrow{1}u\xrightarrow{f}v\xleftarrow{i}y,$$
$$x'\xleftarrow{1}x'\xrightarrow{a}x\xleftarrow{p}u\xrightarrow{f}v\xleftarrow{i}y.$$
The vertical arrows from the first row to the second are $1,p',p,1,1,1$; they are weak equivalences, and the middle square commutes by $pc=ap'$. Reduction of the first row is the pulled-back zigzag, while reduction of the second is precomposition of the original hammock by $a$. For a chain of objects of $\mathcal T$, insert this comparison at each cut of its rows. The pullback maps commute with all original vertical arrows. Deleting and repeating rows commutes with the construction; its prism simplices therefore give the desired homotopy of maps out of $N\mathcal T$. This is precisely the hammock composition of [lem-coef-hammock-infinity-localization].

For $b:y\to y'$, form $v'=v\amalg_y y'$ with $k:v\to v'$ and $i':y'\to v'$. Here $i'$ is the pushout of $i$, hence a trivial cofibration by step 2. The target action is $(p,kf,i')$. The two rows
$$x\xleftarrow{p}u\xrightarrow{f}v\xleftarrow{i}y\xrightarrow{b}y'\xleftarrow{1}y',$$
$$x\xleftarrow{p}u\xrightarrow{f}v\xleftarrow{1}v\xrightarrow{k}v'\xleftarrow{i'}y'$$
have downward vertical arrows $1,1,1,i,i',1$, all weak equivalences; the nontrivial square is $ki=i'b$. Their reductions are respectively postcomposition by $b$ and the pushed-out zigzag. Inserting these rows at the cuts of every chain gives a prism as in step 9. Notice that neither $b$ nor $k$ is required to be a weak equivalence: they are horizontal. The source and target comparisons can be pasted since concatenation and reduction define composition in [lem-coef-hammock-infinity-localization]. Thus simultaneous endpoint changes have the asserted comparisons, with canonical limit/colimit identifications if choices change.

source.place: Remark 3.3 and Lemma 3.4; explicit target-end prism

proof.text: Finally, for $p=i=1$, reduction deletes the two identity outer columns and leaves exactly the length-one hammock of $f$. By [lem-coef-hammock-infinity-localization] this is the map of the localization on $f$. No replacement of either endpoint was made in the proof.
